redactions.original: We hold that petitioner is taxable on the distributions and that a portion of her distributions is subject to the additional tax. But we hold

facts_from_discussion: Petitioner does not contend that any of her IRA contributions were nondeductible when made (no basis; not a Roth IRA).
The record does not show that petitioner was disabled.

The court found petitioner alleged no error by a financial institution that prevented a timely rollover, did not substantiate her contention that a postal error caused the delay, and alleged no disability or similar cause.
The court found petitioner produced no evidence that she set the $15,000 aside for a rollover, or of what she did with the funds or how she used them.

Nearly four years elapsed between petitioner's receipt of the final 2016 distribution and her $15,000 redeposit into her IRA (April 27, 2020); she made no effort to roll over the funds before the notice of deficiency was issued.

The $54,000 figure was Morehouse's estimate of the full-year cost of attendance before any grant or scholarship; petitioner presented no evidence that she actually incurred expenses of that magnitude in 2016.
In the Opinion the court states petitioner reported $24,660 of her distributions as subject to the 10% additional tax (the Findings of Fact say $24,664).
The court found petitioner paid Morehouse $19,092 during 2016: $9,283 distributed directly from her 529 account and $9,809 documented by her bank statements.
The court found that $5,816 of the $9,809 represented the 529-account withdrawals paid to her, leaving $3,993 that petitioner paid Morehouse in 2016 from her IRA withdrawals.

The court found that $3,993 of the $54,500 IRA withdrawals was used during 2016 to pay her son's qualified higher education expenses (tuition and related costs at Morehouse), and that petitioner did not show that any of the remaining IRA withdrawals were used for qualified higher education expenses in 2016.

Petitioner prepared her 2016 return during a very tumultuous time in her life; she reported the full $54,500 of IRA distributions but treated $15,000 as nontaxable because she intended to roll it over.

The court found credible petitioner's testimony that she attempted to report her tax liability correctly, found that she exercised good faith in her reporting, and found that she demonstrated reasonable cause for her underpayment.
Respondent states the penalty was calculated by the IRS automated underreporter (AUR) program; the court made no finding on written supervisory approval.
notes: Rollover waiver (sec. 408(d)(3)(I)) is a mixed fact/equity judgment; only the underlying factual findings were carried over, not the conclusion that waiver was properly denied. The $3,993 QHEE finding is a fact-with-legal-label ('qualified higher education expenses within the meaning of sec. 72(t)(2)(E)'); kept because it is the court's finding of the amount used, but it directly drives the sec. 72(t) result. The reasonable-cause finding is kept per the rules' example even though it effectively decides the penalty.
